metadata.title: TRÚ NEMENDA Á EIGIN GETU OG FRAMMISTAÐA Í STÆRÐFRÆÐILÆSI PISA 2022
metadata.venue: Tímarit um uppeldi og menntun / Icelandic Journal of Education

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for Iceland, where PISA scales and indices are computed using weighted likelihood estimates (weighted likelihood estimates are described for the questionnaire scales). The authors report that the MATHEFF, ANXMAT, and TEACHSUP scales were transformed so that the OECD mean is 0 for comparability, and that scale scores are based on respondents who answered at least three items within each scale. The manuscript does not report applying student sampling weights or replicate weights in the regression analyses, and it instead focuses on regression coefficients and R² from models estimated in R. Given the absence of explicit survey-weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and replicate design details, weighting for complex sampling is not documented for the analytic models, which may affect standard errors and inference under PISA’s clustered design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports PISA 2022 scale construction for MATHEFF, ANXMAT, and TEACHSUP and then estimates multiple regression models predicting mathematics literacy performance, but it does not document how missing responses were handled for the analytic sample (e.g., complete-case vs imputation). Because PISA typically involves missingness across questionnaire items and background variables, the lack of a stated missing-data strategy is a reporting gap that limits reproducibility and may bias estimates if missingness is not handled appropriately.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 data for Iceland; the study states that in Iceland all eligible 15-year-old students were invited and that 3,364 students participated. For the constructed scales (MATHEFF, ANXMAT, TEACHSUP), the authors state that scale scores were computed only for respondents who answered at least three items within the respective scale. No further analytic exclusions (e.g., missing ESCS, missing teacher-support items, or additional grade/school-type restrictions) are explicitly described.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple regression (four nested models): Model 1 R²=0.09 (ESCS β=0.31, p<0.001; Gender β=0.03, p=0.09). Model 2 R²=0.24 (self-efficacy β=0.41, p<0.001). Model 3 R²=0.26 (self-efficacy β=0.36, p<0.001; anxiety β=-0.13, p<0.001). Model 4 R²=0.27 (self-efficacy β=0.34, p<0.001; anxiety β=-0.12, p<0.001; teacher support β=0.11, p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (Iceland) mathematics literacy the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy, mathematics anxiety, teacher support, and socioeconomic status (ESCS) (with gender in the first model) to predict mathematics literacy performance, finding that self-efficacy had a strong positive association (β≈0.34–0.41, p<0.001), mathematics anxiety had a negative association (β≈-0.12 to -0.13, p<0.001), and teacher support showed only a weak positive association (β=0.11, p<0.001) after accounting for self-efficacy and anxiety. This indicates that strengthening students’ mathematics self-efficacy and reducing mathematics anxiety may be more impactful than relying on teacher support alone for improving mathematics achievement, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2022 mathematics literacy performance for Icelandic 15-year-olds (N=3,364) using regression models with PISA-derived scales for mathematics self-efficacy (MATHEFF), mathematics anxiety (ANXMAT), and teacher support (TEACHSUP), alongside ESCS and gender. The authors report nested-model results: ESCS and gender explain 9% of variance (R²=0.09), adding self-efficacy increases explained variance to 24% (self-efficacy β=0.41, p<0.001), and adding anxiety yields R²=0.26 (anxiety β=-0.13, p<0.001). In the full model, teacher support is statistically significant but weak (β=0.11, p<0.001) and the total explained variance is R²=0.27. Limitations include the cross-sectional nature of PISA (no causal identification) and the absence of a documented missing-data handling strategy and explicit complex-survey weighting for the regression inference.
